content: Linezolid has recently been reclassified by the World Health Organization (WHO) as a Group A drug for the treatment of multi-drug resistant tuberculosis (MDR-TB) and extensively drug-resistant tuberculosis (XDR-TB). This classification indicates that linezolid should be included in the treatment regimen for all patients unless there are contraindications. However, the use of linezolid is associated with significant risks of toxicity, and the optimal dosing and duration of treatment remain uncertain. Current treatment guidelines are primarily based on evidence derived from observational, non-comparative studies. The objective of this review was to evaluate the efficacy of linezolid as part of a second-line treatment regimen for MDR and XDR pulmonary tuberculosis. Additionally, the review aimed to assess the prevalence and severity of adverse events associated with linezolid use in this patient population. To gather relevant data, a comprehensive search was conducted across multiple databases, including the Cochrane Infectious Diseases Specialized Register, CENTRAL, MEDLINE, Embase, and LILACS, up to July 13, 2018. Reference lists of articles were also reviewed, and researchers in the field were contacted for additional information. Studies were included if they involved participants who received linezolid and those who did not. Randomized controlled trials (RCTs) were included to evaluate efficacy outcomes, while non-randomized cohort studies were included to assess adverse events. The primary outcomes assessed were all-cause mortality, tuberculosis-associated mortality, treatment failure, and cure rates. Secondary outcomes included treatment interruption, treatment completion, and time to sputum culture conversion. Adverse events were recorded, including their frequency, severity, and whether they led to drug discontinuation or dose reduction. Specific adverse events of interest included neuropathy, anemia, and thrombocytopenia. Two independent reviewers assessed the eligibility of studies and extracted data. Risk of bias was evaluated using the Cochrane Risk of Bias tool for RCTs and the ROBINS-I tool for non-randomized studies. Meta-analysis was not feasible due to the design of one RCT, where participants in the control group received linezolid after a two-month delay, making direct comparisons impossible. Additionally, meta-analysis of non-randomized studies was deemed inappropriate due to heterogeneity. Three RCTs were identified for inclusion. One of these had significant issues with allocation of the study drug and placebo, rendering its data unsuitable for analysis. The remaining two RCTs included 104 participants. One trial randomized 65 participants to receive linezolid or not, in addition to a background regimen. The other trial randomized 39 participants to receive linezolid immediately or after a two-month delay. Fourteen non-randomized cohort studies (two prospective and 12 retrospective) were also included, involving a total of 1,678 participants. These studies were conducted in settings with varying income levels and tuberculosis burdens. Dosing and duration of linezolid therapy varied widely across studies, with daily doses ranging from 300 mg to 1200 mg. Some studies implemented planned dose reductions, while others reported dose reductions inconsistently or not at all. The mean or median duration of linezolid therapy exceeded 90 days in eight of the 14 non-randomized studies that reported this information. Follow-up duration was inconsistently reported, with only five of the 14 non-randomized studies providing this information. The two RCTs were assessed for risk of bias. One trial had a high risk of performance and detection bias but a low risk of attrition bias. The other trial had a low risk of detection and attrition bias for primary outcomes but unclear risks for non-primary outcomes and performance bias. Among the non-randomized studies, three were deemed to have a critical risk of bias, while the remaining 11 had a serious risk of bias. One RCT reported higher cure rates (risk ratio [RR] 2.36, 95% confidence interval [CI] 1.13 to 4.90, very low-certainty evidence), lower treatment failure rates (RR 0.26, 95% CI 0.10 to 0.70, very low-certainty evidence), and higher sputum culture conversion rates at 24 months (RR 2.10, 95% CI 1.30 to 3.40, very low-certainty evidence) in the linezolid-treated group compared to controls. However, this study also reported higher rates of adverse events, including anemia (17/33 versus 2/32), nausea and vomiting, and neuropathy (14/33 versus 1/32) in the linezolid group. Linezolid was discontinued early and permanently in 6.1% (2/33) of participants in this study. The other RCT reported higher sputum culture conversion rates four months after randomization (RR 2.26, 95% CI 1.19 to 4.28) in the group that received linezolid immediately compared to the group with delayed initiation. In this trial, linezolid was discontinued early and permanently in 17.9% (7/39) of participants. In the non-randomized studies, linezolid discontinuation occurred in 22.6% (141/624) of participants across 11 studies. However, due to incomplete data on follow-up duration and the number of participants experiencing adverse events, it was not possible to quantitatively or comparatively summarize total, serious, or linezolid-attributed adverse events. In conclusion, there is some evidence from RCTs supporting the efficacy of linezolid in treating drug-resistant pulmonary tuberculosis, particularly in participants with XDR-TB. However, adverse events and treatment discontinuation were common. The lack of comparative data on efficacy and safety, combined with serious risks of bias and heterogeneity in non-randomized studies, limits the interpretability of existing evidence. Further prospective cohort studies or RCTs, particularly in high tuberculosis burden, low-income, and lower-middle-income countries, are needed to provide more robust data on the efficacy and safety of linezolid as part of treatment regimens for drug-resistant tuberculosis.
